transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Aperture CTO), Marcus Hale (Aperture ML Eng), Priya Singh (Aperture Product)

Summary (auto):
Redwood did a hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, generation params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry semantics and idempotency, and how to tune for latency vs cost. Customer asked about security (SOC2, KMS, VPC), streaming SDKs, and POC benchmarking. Next steps agreed: pricing doc, security artifacts, and a scheduled POC benchmark.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): hey everyone thanks for joining, really appreciate the time. um quick intro from our side, i'm maya chen, i'm the AE on this account and this is samir patel, our solutions engineer.
00:12 Speaker 2 (Samir): hey hi, hi all. i'll be doing most of the demo today. we plan to show hosted api for chat and text gen, streaming, params and retry behaviours.
00:22 Speaker 3 (Lena): thanks maya, thanks samir. quick note, i'm lena, we run infra at aperture. we'll focus on latency and privacy questions — we're healthcare adjacent so HIPAA-ish concerns.
00:30 Speaker 4 (Marcus): marcus here, ml eng, i'll be focused on throughput and cost. we have a mix of batched inference and some low-latency chat features.
00:38 Speaker 5 (Priya): priya from product, i'll be looking at integration complexity and fallbacks.
00:45 Speaker 2 (Samir): great — quick agenda. 1) hosted api overview, 2) live demo of chat + streaming, 3) param tuning (temp, top_p, max_tokens), 4) retry semantics and idempotency keys, 5) Q&A and next steps.
01:10 Speaker 2 (Samir): so Redwood hosted api gives you REST/SDK endpoints for chat and text generation. you can stream responses over chunked responses or websockets depending on SDK. streaming helps reduce time-to-first-token for chat apps.
01:35 Speaker 1 (Maya): one clarification for the team, when we say hosted we mean our managed control plane and runtime with data retention options — you can opt for short retention and encryption keys, or move to dedicated/reserved capacity later if you need isolation.
02:05 Speaker 3 (Lena): quick check, can we use our KMS and keep logs out of your control plane? we want customer-managed keys ideally.
02:15 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, we support KMS integrations for private deployments and for dedicated customers; for hosted we have bring-your-own-key integrations for enterprise tiers — we'll attach the SOC2 docs after.
02:32 Speaker 4 (Marcus): do you support VPC peering or private network endpoints for hosted? we don't want traffic crossing public internet.
02:40 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, there are private endpoint options and regional routing; for strict on-prem you can use Redwood Private. i'll include the network docs.
03:05 Speaker 2 (Samir): ok demo — i'll share my screen. starting with a simple chat call to the hosted api. request body is messages array, model selector, and params like temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop.
03:25 Speaker 2 (Samir): here's a streaming example: we open a connection and receive partial chunks with event frames. this reduces p50 latency because we can start rendering tokens as they arrive.
03:42 Speaker 2 (Samir): // transcribed code sample follows:
03:50 Speaker 2 (Samir): POST /v1/chat/completions
03:55 Speaker 2 (Samir): { "model": "redwood-chat-medium", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the following clinical note..."}], "temperature": 0.2, "max_tokens": 256, "stream": true }
04:20 Speaker 4 (Marcus): small nit — model names, are these open models or redwood-owned? curious about reproducibility and cpu/gpu differences.
04:30 Speaker 2 (Samir): most are curated open models optimized by our runtime. we also provide verified perf profiles so you can pick variants (quantized, fp16) and we show expected tokens/sec and p50 latency in the model catalog.
05:00 Speaker 3 (Lena): how do retries look? if we have intermittent 5xx or timeouts, do we risk double-processing user messages?
05:10 Speaker 2 (Samir): great question — by default we recommend idempotency keys for operations that must be exactly-once. our SDKs send a request-id header and we have retry policies built in. for chat, you can include a client_message_id in the message payload to dedupe.
05:30 Speaker 2 (Samir): retries are configurable — exponential backoff, jitter, and you can configure what errors are retried (transient vs user errors).
06:01 Speaker 5 (Priya): and if we stream and the connection dies mid-response, is there a resume?
06:10 Speaker 2 (Samir): streaming resume is limited; we recommend small chunk windows or using server-side completion with streaming to the client. if you lose connection mid-stream the server may still finish the generation; your client can call the non-streamed endpoint or re-request with the idempotency key to get the final output. there are tradeoffs.
06:45 Speaker 4 (Marcus): can you set temperature per-turn in chat? we want deterministic system messages and more creative user-facing turns.
06:50 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes, you can include per-message params in the messages object or set global params. per-message override is supported in our API.
07:10 Speaker 3 (Lena): security again — logs and auditability. can we get token-level cost logs and per-route latency breakdown?
07:18 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, in Redwood Console you get token-level cost, latency histograms, and trace ids per request. we also emit audit logs and can route them to your SIEM.
07:42 Speaker 5 (Priya): what's the expected latency for small prompts? like 20 tokens response.
07:50 Speaker 2 (Samir): depends on model and batching. for redwood-chat-small we see p50 ~80-120ms in our hosted regions for 20 token responses. with batching there's a tradeoff — batching improves throughput but increases tail latency.
08:15 Speaker 4 (Marcus): what's batching policy look like? do you have continuous batching?
08:22 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes we do continuous batching with smart routing: the runtime keeps a short buffer, batch size is adaptive based on load and latency SLOs, and we optimize kernels based on sequence lengths. you can also pin a route to a dedicated queue to avoid mix with other tenants.
09:00 Speaker 3 (Lena): HIPAA — are you willing to sign a BAA for hosted?
09:07 Speaker 1 (Maya): we have an enterprise compliance package and BAA for qualifying customers; i'll include legal contacts. usually clients with strict HIPAA needs choose dedicated or private.
09:30 Speaker 4 (Marcus): cost question — how do you meter tokens and what about embeddings vs chat?
09:35 Speaker 1 (Maya): usage is token-based for text generation and per-embedding unit for embeddings; the console shows breakdown per route/model. we can show a cost projection for your expected token volume.
10:00 Speaker 2 (Samir): back to demo — here's param tuning. temp = 0 gives deterministic-ish output, 0.7 is more creative. top_p is another knob for nucleus sampling. max_tokens caps the response and is how you control cost.
10:30 Speaker 2 (Samir): here's a live example toggling temperature from 0.2 to 0.8 and you can see the outputs diverge; i'll paste both responses in the chat.
11:05 Speaker 4 (Marcus): what about safety filters and hallucination mitigation? can we run a reranker or classifier pre/post?
11:12 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes, Redwood supports function/tool calling patterns and structured outputs; you can run a lightweight intent classifier or a reranker as a second step. we also have model-based safety layers and you can pin to conservative model variants.
12:00 Speaker 3 (Lena): are there SDKs for streaming in our stack (python/node/java)?
12:06 Speaker 2 (Samir): we have first-class SDKs for Python and Node with streaming helpers; Java SDKs are in beta but we provide examples with raw HTTP/wss so you can integrate quickly.
12:35 Speaker 5 (Priya): with SDK retries and idempotency, does the request cost double if retried? how do we account for that?
12:45 Speaker 2 (Samir): billing counts successful tokens processed; failed or partial attempts are logged but typically not billed as full completions — we'll share the billing policy. for exact accounting we'll provide the breakdown.
13:10 Speaker 4 (Marcus): POC scope — we want to run bench of 100 concurrent chat users, target p95 < 500ms, cost estimate, and safety checks.
13:20 Speaker 1 (Maya): sounds good — we'll propose a POC plan. samir can set up a small benchmark harness and run it in our hosted region or on dedicated nodes if you want lower variance.
13:40 Speaker 3 (Lena): timeline — we need to present to security and legal next week. can we get SOC2 and network docs by tomorrow?
13:48 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes i'll send the SOC2 summary and KMS docs today.
14:05 Speaker 2 (Samir): technical deep-dive: how prefix/KV cache helps cost — if you have repeated prefixes (like system prompts) KV cache keeps key/value attention states to avoid recomputing earlier tokens; this reduces tokens/sec compute and latency for long-running context.
14:35 Speaker 4 (Marcus): good, we use long context notes — prefix caching would help. quantization question: if you use int8 quantization what's the perf delta?
14:45 Speaker 2 (Samir): quantized models (int8) lower GPU memory and cost but can slightly increase latency per-token in some kernels; our runtime picks kernels to optimize for quantized paths. we'll show perf profiles in the catalog.
15:10 Speaker 5 (Priya): about fallbacks — can the system automatically route to a cheaper model when latency spikes or capacity constrained?
15:18 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes, smart routing policies let you route by latency, cost, region, with automatic fallback to compatible variants. you can set SLO triggers for failover.
15:42 Speaker 3 (Lena): what observability do we get during a POC? traces, per-request ids?
15:48 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes, traces, request ids, token-level cost, and sampling of outputs for quality. Console gives dashboards per route/model.
16:10 Speaker 4 (Marcus): sample payload sizes — we need to know network egress for mobile clients.
16:16 Speaker 2 (Samir): we can estimate based on prompt+response tokens; streaming reduces round trips and can lower perceived client bandwidth spikes.
16:45 Speaker 5 (Priya): any limits on concurrent streams or connections?
16:50 Speaker 2 (Samir): hosted has soft limits per account; we can increase them for enterprise or dedicated. for POC we'll ensure quota is sufficient.
17:15 Speaker 3 (Lena): legal question — retention windows and deletion APIs?
17:21 Speaker 1 (Maya): retention configurable; we also have deletion APIs and audit logs for data access. for strict compliance we recommend dedicated or private with customer-managed keys.
18:00 Speaker 2 (Samir): quick demo of retry example: show a simulated transient 503, client retries with exponential backoff and an idempotency key, server returns the same completion token id so client dedups.
18:35 Speaker 4 (Marcus): can you show how to set idempotency in the SDK?
18:40 Speaker 2 (Samir): sure — example header X-Request-Id: <uuid> or parameter client_message_id in messages.
19:15 Speaker 5 (Priya): also curious about multi-turn context size — how do you manage token budget across turns?
19:22 Speaker 2 (Samir): you can use summarization + embeddings to compress earlier turns, or tune truncation strategies. Optimize has recommendations for batching and caching to reduce cost.
20:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): we didn't dive deep into Redwood Optimize but that product gives batching/caching suggestions and quantization recommendations based on your workload. it can simulate cost tradeoffs.
20:30 Speaker 3 (Lena): ok high level this looks promising. can you send a clear doc with pros/cons of hosted vs dedicated for our legal/infra team?
20:38 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, pricing + hosted vs dedicated comparison will be in the email.
21:05 Speaker 2 (Samir): quick note about SDK logs — you'll get correlation ids to join traces from client to server.
21:30 Speaker 4 (Marcus): uhh, about failover to other regions — do you support cross-region fallback if a region has issues?
21:36 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes, smart routing can fallback to another region or model variant. consistency of model weights is something to consider, we'll note that in the runbook.
22:10 Speaker 5 (Priya): question on deployment modes — if we start hosted and later move to dedicated, how hard is migration?
22:18 Speaker 2 (Samir): the API and model routing abstraction is the same. you can pin model versions and rollout policies; migration is largely config and routing changes, validating perf in dedicated environment.
23:00 Speaker 3 (Lena): are there reference architectures for hybrid where PII goes to private and other traffic is hosted?
23:06 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes we have hybrid patterns — prefix routing, tokenization and client-side redaction, plus private endpoints for sensitive workloads.
23:40 Speaker 4 (Marcus): cost projection — can you provide a back-of-envelope for 1M tokens/month?
23:46 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, i'll include a sample spreadsheet; pricing depends on model class and whether you're on hosted or dedicated.
24:10 Speaker 2 (Samir): moving to the last demo slide — network diagrams and how streaming works end-to-end with the SDK.
24:40 Speaker 3 (Lena): ok good, any known issues with our stack (we're on AWS ECS, internal KMS)?
24:48 Speaker 2 (Samir): that's a common stack — private endpoints and KMS integration are supported; for very strict keys we recommend dedicated or private.
25:20 Speaker 5 (Priya): do you have examples for conversation UI with streaming?
25:25 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes we have a web-demo repo showing client-side token rendering and partial response stitching.
26:00 Speaker 4 (Marcus): what's the expected time to onboard — we have developers ready now.
26:06 Speaker 1 (Maya): self-serve get started is minutes to sign up, POC with benchmark can be initiated within a few days with our help. enterprise contracts for BAAs or dedicated often take longer.
26:45 Speaker 3 (Lena): ok let's confirm next steps.
26:50 Speaker 1 (Maya): recap: 1) i'll send pricing + hosted vs dedicated doc and SOC2/security whitepaper; 2) samir will prepare the POC runbook and benchmark harness; 3) apertures team will share prompt set and SLOs. we tentatively scheduled 2026-07-22 for the benchmark run.
27:20 Speaker 4 (Marcus): yes we'll share the prompt set and target latencies by tomorrow.
27:30 Speaker 5 (Priya): please include sample code for streaming in node and python.
27:35 Speaker 2 (Samir): will do.
27:50 Speaker 1 (Maya): any final questions?
28:00 Speaker 3 (Lena): none from me, thank you.
28:10 Speaker 4 (Marcus): thanks all.
28:15 Speaker 5 (Priya): thanks, that's helpful.
28:20 Speaker 1 (Maya): great, we'll follow up via email and upload artifacts to the shared drive.
28:30 Speaker 2 (Samir): end of recorded portion — post-call small notes: discussed potential dedicated early if legal pushes hard, and Redwood Optimize could save 20-40% on token cost for their workload per our estimates (ballpark).
